articles.text: Reports from Nebraska state that the recent storm will occasion severe loss on cattle. In places, the telegraph lines were down for several days, it being impossible for linemen to face the storm.
articles.summary: Nebraska storm expected to cause severe cattle losses.

articles.text: Specials from Montreal express great fear that there will soon be another uprising on the part of the half-breeds and Indians. They are now plentifully supplied with ammunition, the lack of which they think was the cause of their former failure.
articles.summary: Montreal reports fear of a new half-breed and Indian uprising.

articles.text: Sections of Texas, notably Galveston, Austin, Laredo, Palestine and Corpus Christi report the coldest weather in forty years. There will be great loss on stock but as yet it is too early to estimate it.
articles.summary: Texas reports coldest weather in forty years and expected stock losses.

articles.text: The manufacturers of barbed wire have formed a combination for the purpose of raising prices. Within a few days the price has advanced sixty cents a hundred and a further advance is contemplated.
articles.summary: Barbed-wire makers combine to raise prices.

articles.text: Vol. 1, No. 3, of the Buffalo Gap Advance comes to us with boom! BOOM!! BOOM!!! all over it. The Advance prophesies permanency for the town and with good reason for it is a natural supply point to a large country. The boom times will probably leave it in the spring, however.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy notices the third number of the Buffalo Gap Advance.

articles.text: The death of Hon. John B. Raymond of Fargo, was curiously foretold by a Norwegian woman who worked on his farm. A turkey was accidentally killed on Christmas day and she was greatly effected thereat, declaring that either Mr. Raymond or one of his family would soon die. It seems strange that coincidence should so often come to the aid of superstition.
articles.summary: Death of John B. Raymond of Fargo said to have been foretold by a farm worker.

articles.text: Land commissioner Sparks and Pension commissioner Black are the two shining lights of humbuggery of the present administration. It transpires that Black, who is a strong, healthy man in the perfection of physical development, draws the largest pension of any old soldier because, according to his own statement he is a "physical wreck, without the use of either arm." It would be a blessing if some patriot would make a "physical wreck" of him.
articles.summary: Packard attacks Land Commissioner Sparks and Pension Commissioner Black.

articles.text: The meeting for the organization of a National range stockgrowers' association will be held in Denver on Jan. 27. Unless cool and cautious heads are allowed to rule, this convention may do more harm than anything from which the range industries have ever suffered. The eastern press will narrowly watch proceedings, and mole-hills will be magnified into mountains in adversely criticizing the "rapacity of the cattle kings." Properly conducted, it will be a means of the greatest good to rangemen, as there has never been any united action among them of a national character.
articles.summary: Packard urges caution at the coming Denver meeting to organize a national range stockgrowers' association.

articles.text: The list of victories of the "Bonnie Black Doddies," published in another column, is of especial interest to all range cattlemen. When we add to this list of victories over all other breeds for all purposes the fact that they are par excellence for range purposes, we have a combination of good traits that stamps the Aberdeen-Angus as beyond question the range animal of the future. Those that have been brought into the Bad Lands, notably those of the Maltese cross outfit, are now in the pink of condition and are apparently as contented with the thermometer forty degrees below as they are when it is forty degrees above zero.
articles.summary: Packard calls the Aberdeen-Angus the range animal of the future, noting the Maltese cross outfit's Angus are thriving in the Bad Lands cold.

articles.text:
The following letter, received by Bob Roberts, probably contains a plain, unvarnished account of Alaska and shows how magnified are the reports from that country. It would be well for those who contemplate going there to "look before they leap."

Juneau, Alaska.
Dec. 17, 1885.

Friend Bob:—

You were anxious to find out something about this country and I will try and inform you to the best of my ability. The biggest excitement here now is the Yakon country but so far there is nothing discovered there yet outside of some bar diggings on the rivers and they pay from $5 to $10 a day to the man. But that Yakon country is a big country and I am in hopes that in a couple of years more they will strike something worth going after but so far they have not got it and what little they have found is in British Columbia under the English government. There is more going on here than in any other part of Alaska. This summer they just completed the finest mill I suppose in the world at an expense of three hundred and fifty thousand for the mill alone, but it will not take them long to get out money at the [illegible] have been doing since they started, [illegible] yet there is nobody that knows for certain how much they are taking out. They have one hundred and twenty stamps running on the mill and use from 300 to 350 tons of ore every twenty-four hours, the ore averages about five dollars at the least. Their actual expenses when things are running in good shape will be about $1.25 a ton for mining and milling so that gives them a profit of $3.75 a ton that is as near as you can get to it and next summer they are almost sure to put up another mill like this. But this company with lots of money that they had and are making now, have the best of the country right here corralled to themselves and outside of what they have got there is nothing done or being done in this place at all. They are working about forty white men on the mine and mill all told, the rest are Chinamen and Indians. There is a little placer mining camp about three miles from here, and in the summer a few white men work there but now all is idle for the winter. There are about four or five hundred white men and women in and around this place and that is about one-half of the population of all Alaska. It is doubtful if there are a thousand in the whole country, still the governor in his report has put it a good deal higher. I beleive there are some doing pretty well in the fur business. But that big fur company has that pretty well to themselves the same as anything else. There are a few Indians here maybe two or three hundred and some of them are at work, the rest do nothing and live on dried salmon. That is pretty near all their support, the Indians here are different from those around where you are. These will work and some of them do work from one end of the year to the other. No whiskey is allowed to be brought into the country but yet there are about twenty saloons in Junean alone and all selling is as public as in New York city, the only trouble is in getting it in and a good deal is manufactured right here, and the Indians are the worst you ever saw. If a white man gives them any whiskey they are liable to go right straight to the first officer they can find and tell him who gave it to them, so you can judge there is not much of that done. There is civil law here now, and some one is hauled up every day or two. So on the whole I would not advise you to come here and invest anything in the country at the present time. Still there are men here that are going to make money, and others again after bringing considerable money into the country will leave it broke. But that is the way with mostly every mining camp and excitement. Undoubtedly there will be a good deal of money taken out of here for years to come, but the work will be done by Chinamen and Indians and that will not help the country any. This country has got the meanest weather you ever saw, raining or snowing all the time but it is not cold, the rain or snow does not stop any one from working outside. Sometimes it never stops raining for two weeks at a time.

Your dear friend,
Owen Jones.
articles.summary: Letter from Owen Jones at Juneau to Bob Roberts of Medora giving a sober account of Alaska mining prospects.

articles.headline: The Bonnie Black Doddies.
articles.text:
The season of the fat-stock shows is over and the final contests of the year decided. Let us take a summary view of the whole and see what part the Aberdeen-Angus have taken in the fray, in competition with the other breeds.

We will commence at Riverview park, Kansas City, Mo., and wind up at Islington hall, London, England. At Kansas City, the doddies were only represented by six animals out of 108 of all other breeds that were represented. The first winnings the blacks could compete for, outside of their own class was, "Sweepstakes All Breeds," early maturity. In class for steer or spayed heifer, two years and under three, we find the Aberdeen-Anguns steers Blaine and Logan stand first and second. In the one-year-old class Messers. Gudgell & Simpson win with that marvelous steer Sandy, and in class under one year old the same gentlemen win first with their Angus steer calf Alex, while Messers Estill & Flliot take second place with their calf Felix. Here plain out, the Aberdeen-Angus make a clean sweep of all the early-maturity classes wherever they competed.

Let us visit Chicago, the American Smithfield; here the blacks appear even more microscopical in numbers, yet they fill a proud position. Mr. J. J. Hill's Aberdeen-Angus steer Benholm wins the consolation stakes as best two-year-old, and Messors. Gudgell & Simpson's Sandy is first in the yearling class, both in competition with a strong array of good ones of all breeds. Mr. Hill's black steer Turiff sustains the reputation of the Scots by winning the $75 prize as best three-year-old carcass of any breed. He too comes in first for carcass prize showing greatest amount of edible beef. Their honors do not rest here, as Mr. Hill's Angus steer Benholm makes the highest per cent of dressed to gross weight, 71.4 being the highest given by any beast of any age. Noble doddies! here again you sustain your last year's reputation, reflecting additional lustre upon the fame of the Aberdeen-Angus as prime butchers' [illegible] It will be interesting to compare weights of various cross-breeds at Chicago. Twelve grade Herefords, shown at an average age of three years, six months and five days, give an average weight of 2,070 lbs., an average gain per day from birth of less than 1.60 lbs. Thirteen grade Short-horns, at an average age of three ytars, six months and sixteen days, show an average weight of 2,037 lbs., an average gain per day from birth of less than 1.58 lbs. The three cross-bred Angus shown by Mr. Hill out-do either Short-horn or Heroford grades. At an average age of three years, four months and nineteen days, give an average weight of over 2,271 lbs., with an average gain per day from birth of 1.88 lbs. The Angus crosses are over 200 lbs. heavier than that of either the Short-horn or Herefoad, are two months younger, and make a greater gain per day, another invaluable triumph for Angus blood.

Let us visit Rutland show held at Oakham, one of England's best cattle districts. In the class of oxen other than Short-horn, three years old, we find the first and second winners are Aberdeen-Angus crosses; the third prize is a pure-bred polled ox. In class of steers of any breed, three years, the prize is won by Mr. Stephenson with his pure-bred ox, Sultan. The second and third prizes were won by polled crosses also. In the two-year-old class, open to all breeds, Mr. Stephenson again figures with his pure Aberdeen ox, Freedom. In class of best heifer of any breed, Mr. Stephenson is an easy winner with his charming Aberdeen-Angus heifer, Luxury, of ancient lineage. What a success the black blood proves to be! What of the Yorkshire society's fat-stock exhibition, held at Yorkshire? In class for cross-bred oxen not exceeding four years old, there is keen competition, yet all in favor of black blood. Mr. Curry wins first and Mr. Wallis second with two admirable Aberdeen-Angus crosses. The highest award on cross-bred cow or heifer class was allotted to a daughter of the [Erica?] bull, Escourt.

At Birmingham, we are told, there was a splendid show of Scotch cattle and as not infrequently happens, the highest honors of the day fell to them. We will merely notice their winnings in competition with other breeds. The champion ox again is a black polled cross, property of Mr. Robert Loder. He was placed champion at Norwich, but at Birmingham he wins a special prize of $250 as the best cross-bred animal in the show. This steer was by a Short-horn bull from a polled cow; let his sire have a share in the honor. Mr. Loder's ox weighed 2,624 bounds, a younger steer than the Chicago Regulus, yet weighing 334 pounds more, showing the decided superiority of the Aberdoon-Angus and Short-horn cross to that of the Hereford and Short-horn. In class of two-year-old cross-bred oxen, the Duchess of Sutherland is victorious, with a gray ox by an Angus sire and Mr. Stephenson ranks high with a black polled ox. In the yearling class, a cross by the polled bull Proud Knight is winner.

Thirteen were entered in the cross-bred cow or heifer class. Black blood comes to the front once more, Flora MacDonald is winner, she the produce of a renowned Aberdeen-Angus sire. The butchers of Birmingham present a prize for the best animal for butchers' purposes of not less than seventeen hundred weight. Guess who won it? Mr. Cridlan's pure Aberdeen-Angus ox did, weighing at three years, 2,215 pounds; a proud victory indeed. Now for that much-coveted trophy, the Elkington Challenge vase. Who wins it? A doddie, of course! Mr. Clement Stephenson's charming, sleek, black, Aberdeen-Angus heifer Luxury wins the great prize over 209 of England's choicest animals, her live weight 1,724 pounds.

Now ror the grand wind-up, Smithfield, a repetition of black victories. The blacks are all-conquering. We read that the blacks contain by far the grandest display. Flora MacDonald, a two-year-old polled cross was brought to the front and received the silver cup as the best cross-bred anemal in the yard. Finally the greatest prize is decided and Mr. Stephenson's Aberdeen-Angus heifer Luxury, amid the greatest excitement and enthusiasm is declared the champion; the bucolic queen of the day. For three years in succession Mr. Stephenson has won the Elkington vase, valued at $500. In every case it has been won by black polled two-year-old heifers.

Such victories are unprecedented in the annals of show-yard history. Never, during the eighty-eight years of the Smithfield club have such honors been approached by any other breed.—[Wm Watson in Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: Reprinted survey (Wm Watson, Breeder's Gazette) of Aberdeen-Angus victories at the 1885 fat-stock shows in America and England.

articles.text: Major W. Aug. Fonda, who paralyzed the Bad Lands a year ago by his atrocious puns, has received his commission as postmaster at Stanton, the county seat of Mercer county.
articles.summary: Major W. Aug. Fonda commissioned postmaster at Stanton.

articles.text: The bulls at the Logging camp are in fine condition. They have comfortable stables and the best of care. Where an outfit takes care of its own bulls, it is undoubtedly the best plan to house them well, as the loss is reduced to a minimum and the feed that would otherwise go toward keeping up animal heat is consumed directly in making flesh.
articles.summary: Bulls wintering at the Logging camp are in fine condition.

articles.text: Last Friday morning was a "screamer." The spirit thermometers nearly knocked the eye out of fifty below, while the mercury thermometers might as well have been in business in Patagonia as far as any good they did here was concerned. There was no wind and it was much more comfortable than the day before when it was twenty-five degrees warmer but windy.
articles.summary: Last Friday morning spirit thermometers neared fifty below at Medora.

articles.text: The cold weather of Thursday night was too much for one Maltese cross and one LC bull at the Big plateau camp. They were the weaklings of the herd and it was scarcely expected they would live the winter out although they had gained encouragingly since being taken up. Continued severe weather may result in the loss of a few others, but it would not be surprising if there was not another loss.
articles.summary: Cold of Thursday night killed one Maltese cross and one LC bull at the Big plateau camp.

articles.text: Since last Thursday we have had occasion to revise our figures on the number of deer killed in the Bad Lands tributary to Medora. The number is certainly over 1,500 and probably will come nearer 2,000. It seems scarcely possible, but this is the smallest winter's killing in four years. The cream of the hunting is gone forever and as many weary hunters who have tramped all day and scarcely seen a track can testify, the man who kills a deer will earn it.
articles.summary: Deer killed this winter in the Bad Lands tributary to Medora revised to 1,500-2,000, the smallest in four years.

articles.text:
The following we clip from the Milwaukee Daily Journal. It alludes to Vic Smith and his brother Bill, under the names of Yellowstone Vic and Montana Bill. A letter from Vic states that they are having a jolly time at a big salary:

"The fancy rifle shooting of the two scouts, now at the Dime museum, is an exhibition of wonderful skill. 'Yellowstone Vic' is performing some wonderful feats. Last evening he snuffed a candle at seven or eight paces, held between the teeth of his companion, Montana Bill. The candle was only two inches long.—[Glendive Times.
articles.summary: Vic Smith and his brother Bill performing rifle shooting at a Milwaukee dime museum.

articles.text: The "Blonde butcher," Cranston, who will be remembered as working here last summer, bit off more than he could chew in Chicago recently. He was to have a hard glove contest with a man named Ware in the Stock yards theater. Elaborate preparations and announcements were made. According to the Inter Ocean: "Ware forced the fighting from the start with a stinging blow on Cranston's jaw. The latter fled to his corner, closely pressed by Ware and before the first round closed, jumped over the ropes and escaped."
articles.summary: Cranston, the 'Blonde butcher' formerly of Medora, fled a glove contest in Chicago.

articles.text: Tomorrow is the time fixed by Judge Carpenter for a hearing in the matter of the Luffsey estate. Luffsey is the hunter who was killed in 1883 at Medora in a melee in which the Marquis de Mores was engaged. A. N. McGindley was appointed administrator. The question involved is as to how the estate should be distributed. There are two claims, one for burial expenses, and one of O'Donnell the hunter, companion of Luffsey, who claims to have been a partner of Luffsey's in the estate. The matter is now under consideration by Judge Carpenter and will doubtless be decided in a very few days.—[Mandan Pioneer.
articles.summary: Judge Carpenter to hear the Luffsey estate matter; Luffsey was killed in 1883 in a melee involving the Marquis de Mores.

articles.text: On account of the Bismarck opposition to the organization of Billings county, we see no way of avoiding the payment of taxes to Stark county, which become delinquent on Feb 1. After this date a penalty of five per cent. is added. There is grave doubt as to the constitutionality of the law authorizing the levying of this tax and we earnestly advise that all taxes should be paid to Stark county under protest. Then a test case can decide the constitutionality of the law and should it be decided in our favor, there will be no difficulty in recovering our money. The expense of a test case will be very slight proportionately and upon the receipt of good legal opinion that the law can be declared unconstitutional we will issue a call for a meeting to take steps in the matter. Pending this, it will certainly be safer and may avoid a five per cent penalty to pay under protest before Feb. 1.
articles.summary: Packard advises paying Stark county taxes under protest before Feb. 1 given Bismarck's opposition to organizing Billings county.
